assessments.name: RSA
assessments.threatSummary: Shor's polynomial-time algorithm completely undermines RSA (integer factorization / discrete logarithm). Private keys and ciphertexts are broken once a Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) is realized.

recommendation.transitionStrategy: Determine downstream key pair use: migrate to ML-DSA/SLH-DSA if used for signatures; migrate to ML-KEM if used for key encapsulation.
recommendation.nistGuidanceRationale: KeyPairGenerator for RSA generates classical asymmetric keys vulnerable to Shor's algorithm. Intended application usage (signature vs key exchange vs encryption) is undetermined at this key generation site. Do not assume ML-KEM without establishing key usage.

assessments.name: RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-512AndMGF1Padding
assessments.threatSummary: Shor's polynomial-time algorithm completely undermines RSA (integer factorization / discrete logarithm). Private keys and ciphertexts are broken once a Cryptanalytically Relevant Quantum Computer (CRQC) is realized.

recommendation.transitionStrategy: Re-architect message encryption to encapsulate a symmetric key using ML-KEM, then encrypt payload using AES-256-GCM.
recommendation.nistGuidanceRationale: RSA public-key encryption (RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-512AndMGF1Padding) is completely broken by Shor's algorithm. Note: NIST FIPS 203 ML-KEM is a Key Encapsulation Mechanism, not a direct drop-in Cipher replacement for arbitrary plaintext. Re-architect to encapsulate a symmetric key using ML-KEM, then encrypt payload using AES-256-GCM.

assessments.name: SHA1PRNG
assessments.threatSummary: SHA1PRNG security depends on the runtime security provider and seeding mechanism. The Sun/Oracle JDK provider securely seeds from OS entropy (/dev/urandom or Windows CryptoAPI) and is not broken; however, legacy Android Apache Harmony implementations had critical state-replacement flaws. Provider verification is required.

recommendation.transitionStrategy: Verify runtime security provider in java.security; upgrade to SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong() or SHA-256-based DRBG.
recommendation.nistGuidanceRationale: SHA1PRNG is not intrinsically broken on modern JDKs when seeded from OS entropy (/dev/urandom or CryptoAPI). However, legacy providers (e.g. Apache Harmony) have known state-replacement vulnerabilities. SetSeed() must not be used to replace entropy. Audit provider configuration and migrate to NIST SP 800-90A DRBG.

assessments.name: DES
assessments.threatSummary: Algorithm is broken or deprecated under classical cryptanalysis (e.g. collision attacks, small key/block size). Insecurity is fundamentally classical, not quantum.

recommendation.transitionStrategy: Replace deprecated algorithm immediately to remediate known classical vulnerabilities (not solely a quantum concern).
recommendation.nistGuidanceRationale: Legacy algorithm (DES) is broken or deprecated under classical cryptanalysis. Immediate classical vulnerability remediation is required regardless of quantum timelines.

assessments.name: AES
assessments.threatSummary: Grover's quantum search algorithm provides quadratic speedup for key search O(2^(k/2)). AES-256 retains 128-bit quantum security; AES-128 drops to 64-bit.

recommendation.transitionStrategy: Enforce minimum 256-bit symmetric key length to guarantee at least 128-bit post-quantum security.
recommendation.nistGuidanceRationale: Grover's algorithm provides quadratic speedup against symmetric key search. AES-256 maintains 128 bits of post-quantum security margin.

assessments.name: SHA-512
assessments.threatSummary: Grover provides quadratic speedup for preimages O(2^(n/2)); quantum collision attacks (BHT) are constrained by severe QRAM hardware bounds. Hashes remain robust.

recommendation.transitionStrategy: Maintain modern SHA-2/SHA-3 hashes; use SHA-384 or SHA-512 for conservative post-quantum margins.
recommendation.nistGuidanceRationale: Grover's algorithm provides quadratic speedup for preimages O(2^(n/2)); quantum collision finding (BHT) is bounded by O(2^(n/3)) but constrained by extreme QRAM requirements. SHA-256/384/512 remain robust; use SHA-384 or SHA-512 for conservative post-quantum margins.
